content: The United Kingdom has a statutory notification system for infectious diseases. Under this system, medical doctors are legally obligated to notify a Proper Officer of the local authority, such as a Consultant in Communicable Disease Control, whenever they encounter a case of a serious infectious disease, such as diphtheria or measles. The Proper Officer is then responsible for reporting the case to the Centre for Infections of the Health Protection Agency, located in Colindale, London. The primary objective of this system is to detect and intervene in potential epidemics. Additionally, it facilitates the collection of surveillance data, which can be used to develop strategies for preventing future outbreaks. The statutory requirement for the notification of certain infectious diseases was first introduced in London in 1891. At that time, diseases such as cholera, diphtheria, smallpox, and typhoid had to be reported by the head of the family or the landlord to the local authority. By 1899, this system had been extended to the rest of England and Wales. Initially, disease statistics were collected from local authorities by the Registrar General's Office, which was already responsible for compiling national statistics on births, marriages, and deaths. This office later became known as the Office of Population Censuses and Surveys and is now referred to as the Office for National Statistics. In 1997, the responsibility for administering the notification system was transferred to the Communicable Disease Surveillance Centre (CDSC). In its modern form, the system prioritizes the rapid detection of potential outbreaks, with diagnostic accuracy being a secondary concern. Since 1968, a clinical suspicion of a notifiable infection has been sufficient to report a case. The attending physician is required to notify the Proper Officer, who is typically a Consultant in Communicable Disease Control. These consultants are obligated to inform the CDSC on a weekly basis about each notified case. The CDSC compiles these reports and publishes analyses of local and national trends. The current list of notifiable diseases includes 30 conditions, such as leprosy, which must be reported directly to the director of the CDSC. During the 2002-2003 outbreak, SARS was added to the list as the 31st notifiable disease.
